utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-98-32-T, the Prosecutor versus Mitar Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Pavlovic, good morning. Mrs. Pavlovic, we will resume where we broke off yesterday afternoon. If you remember, we were discussing the organisation of work that you had at your department, the nurses' shifts and the records you kept. So let us pick up there. Having explained yesterday how the shifts worked, could you tell us how you kept the records about those shifts?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean where we wrote down the patients, the newly admitted patients?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: What I meant was, what entries did you make in that notebook?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When a patient comes to the ward, he brings with him the case history in which the particulars have already been entered, that is, the name, surname, the name of one parent, where he comes from, his ID number under which he has been registered in the admissions department, because -- which is the most important number because it is a reference number for everything else we do, his blood count, when he goes into surgery, when any tests are made. So we write down the patient's name and this ID number of the patient.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you write down also the room number of the patient?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we write down the room to which he has been admitted, his first and last name, what the doctor who admitted him -- which tests the doctor wants done, and as I said, the ID or registration number of the patient.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: The number that you have mentioned as the registration number, is that a number given to each patient individually so that during that year, no one else can have the same number or can that number be accorded to someone else later?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is the number for that patient only. It is his registration number which cannot be allotted to anyone else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Madam, may I remind you to pause before you start your answer to enable the interpreters to catch up. You came in immediately after the question there, right over the translation. So please remember to pause.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That's all right. It's very easy to forget. I see that the screen has been put on. You'll see the typing on it. That is the English translation, so that gives you a pretty good idea of where the translators or the interpreters are up to. So wait for the typing to finish before you answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: The number that you were talking about, is such a number given to each patient of the general hospital regardless of which department they're in? Is it a number that is applied to patients regardless of the wards to which they have been admitted?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That number is given to every patient who is admitted to hospital, regardless of which department he is in. So that is a number allotted to that patient only.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Where is that number attributed, in your department or somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The number is attributed at the admissions department when the patient is admitted, because every patient has to report to the admissions if he's being hospitalised. Then his name is entered in a book that is kept over there and that is when he's allotted a number. Upon admission, therefore.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: In your hospital, was there a register of patients for a particular year by alphabetical order?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that because no such ledger was kept in my department.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: The records you mentioned, that is, the notebooks that were kept by the shifts for this particular period, you have them even though it has been such a long time ago?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There are many people who come to our ward needing various data from us. So in agreement with the head of our department, we decided to keep those notebooks for 1992 and 1993 until further notice.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, you have kept those notebooks even though you were not obliged to do so by law.

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right. We need to safekeep those notebooks, according to the laws of our country, for two years.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You have brought with you to The Hague two such notebooks; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've brought them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I will show you now a notebook from this particular period, so will you be kind enough to look at it and to look at two copies of the pages that I have some questions about. So will you please look at them. In view of the fact that you've brought two books, will you please look which one relates to June 1992.

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is from the beginning of 1992, January, and then it continues on. This is the notebook which starts out from -- these are two notebooks covering all patients admitted in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Would you please read out the dates for the first book and the second book.

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first book is from the 9th of January, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Until what date? Until what date?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until the 9th of October -- I'm sorry, the 7th. The 9th of July, 1992. Then the second book starts from the 10th of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: There was an error in your answer and in the transcript. The dates for the first book and the second.

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first book ended with the 10th of July, 1992, with the third shift, and the second book begins with the second shift of the 10th of July, 1992. And it goes on until the 22nd of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Will you please look at the first book as it relates to the relevant period, the one which covered the period up to the 10th of July, 1992, and will you please tell us whether that is the notebook that was kept by nurses?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is that notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Will you please look at the page for the 14th of June, 1992. And to make it easier for you, I will provide copies of that page for you and the Court. I've already provided the interpreters with copies, and there are sufficient copies here for everyone. Mr. Groome was served this copy two days ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Is there a translation of it?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I think that Mr. Groome had a translation. For two days I couldn't have a translation, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Is this one of the four pages you said were the only ones left?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Just first of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Have you got a translation, Mr. Groome, even a rough one?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I have a rough translation, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You proceed, Mr. Domazet. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Pavlovic, have you found this page?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Will you please read out what it says in that book of yours regarding the third shift on the 14th of June, 1992? Will you please read it out slowly, and then I'll have some questions for you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The third shift, the 14th/15th of June, 1992. In the course of the shift, Mitar Vasiljevic, room 413, was admitted. He's being administered the prescribed therapy. The rest of it has been distributed on time. Mulahmetovic in room 414 has a temperature of 38.8 degrees Celsius. He has received Novalgetol injection. For Filipovic, 413, blood test has to be made of glucemia and hematocrit at 0500 hours. Patients present, 54. The shift is handed over by Nada, Milena, and Damir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, it may assist us, I think, if we knew what is regarded as the usual duty hours of the third shift.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Pavlovic, I think you spoke about that yesterday, but could you please tell us once again how the shifts were organised, that is, how long they lasted?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the third shift, or all shifts?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: All shifts, madam.

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first shift starts at 6.00 a.m. and ends at 1.00 p.m. The second shift begins at 1.00 p.m. and goes on until 8.00 p.m. The third shift starts at 8.00 p.m. and ends the next day at 6.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Was this kind of schedule always applied or did it change?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Always, ever since I have been working at the orthopaedics department.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Would the schedule be identical or similar in other departments? Since you have only been working at the orthopaedic department, do you know that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot be certain, but I think that is how shifts are organised in other departments as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So, Mrs. Pavlovic, what you just read out was about the third shift on the night of the 14th to the 15th of June, 1992, the shift that started at 8.00 p.m. on the 14th and ended at 6.00 a.m. on the 15th; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: According to what you read out, Mitar Vasiljevic was admitted and put up in room 413. I'd like to know what is this note made about patient Filipovic? What does it mean?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Patient Filipovic was admitted on the same day but in the course of the second shift. I think he was taken to the surgery immediately and the anaesthesiologist requested certain tests to be made, and that is why it was the duty of the third shift to write down everything that needed to be done in the course of the next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Does that mean that this Filipovic was operated before the third shift started?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is what it means.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You told us that this patient Filipovic was admitted on the 14th of June but in the second shift. Is this something that is noted in this notebook?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Here, I have found it. I have it noted down in the notebook. The second shift, the 14th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Will you please tell us, the words at the end of this paragraph, shift handed over and three names. Who are those people, will you tell us, please? What were they doing in those days?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean my colleagues who handed over the third shift?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, Mrs. Pavlovic.

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My colleague Nada is no longer working in our department. In the meantime, she fell ill. She's a psychiatric patient. Milena has left. She never contacted us. She's working somewhere abroad. And Damir, a man, he's still in our department.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So these are nurses and Damir is a medical technician. Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: From your notebook we see that there are entries only about the second and third shifts; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I think you explained yesterday why there is no reference to the first shift in this book.

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Should I repeat the explanation?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: No. It's not necessary, madam. Mrs. Pavlovic, looking through this notebook, the original one that you brought with you, there is an entry for the third shift between the 4th and the 5th of July, 1992, where the name of Mitar Vasiljevic appears. Could you find that page, please?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I'd like to give you a photostat of that page.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I also have copies for the Court. Could I ask the usher for his assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: What do you want done with the page which we've already dealt with?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like it to be entered into evidence, but I was going to suggest at the end the tendering of the book and these photostats.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: All right then. As long as we don't forget it. Do you have a translation of it there, Mr. Groome? I'm sorry to be asking you all the time for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You have in the other page of this translation from Mr. Groome, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: The one that we've already got, is it? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We still haven't got these documents that you've just handed up. Can we have a copy of this document, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mrs. Pavlovic, have you looked at that page and the photocopy of that page? So will you please read out what has been noted in your book for the third shift between the 4th and the 5th of July, 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Third shift, between the 4th and the 5th of July, 1992. There are 34 patients. No new admissions. No one had a high temperature. Therapy has been distributed, instruments sterilised. There are three thermometers. The shift is handed over by Nada, Vesko and Buba. PS: Mitar Vasiljevic needs to be cautioned about his behaviour (singing loudly, taking other people's belongings).

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mrs. Pavlovic, next to the name of Mitar Vasiljevic there is a number. Will you look, please? What does that number mean?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the number of the room in which he was, room 411.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Does that mean, Mrs. Pavlovic, that he was moved from one room to another during his hospitalisation since on the previous page that you read out for the 14th of June, I think you said that he was admitted to room 413?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was admitted to 413, and probably because there wasn't room in 411 on that day or that night, because it is a room that is supervised by Dr. Dusko Jovicevic, rooms 411 and 412. And as soon as there was a vacant bed, he was immediately transferred to room 411, and he remained in that room for as long as he stayed at our department.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you said there were rooms of a certain doctor, in this case Dr. Jovicevic, what does that mean? Does that mean that they were patients that were operated by that doctor, that were cared by that doctor, or something else?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In our department, every doctor has rooms that he supervises, and we admit patients to those rooms that were admitted by that doctor, regardless of whether they are for surgery or not. In the event that there is no room in his rooms, then it is possible, it is admitted -- allowed to admit a patient to the room supervised by another doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Does that mean, Mrs. Pavlovic, that Dr. Jovicevic was the doctor who admitted Mitar Vasiljevic to the orthopaedics department on the 14th of June, 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was on duty that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you looked at the book a moment ago and looking at it again, who wrote these notes? Because the shift was handed over by three individuals. Was it always one person who wrote down the comments that took place during a shift?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They would agree -- the nurses would agree amongst themselves. Do you want me to tell you who wrote this entry, this addition for the third shift between the 4th and 5th of July? Would you like me to tell you who wrote that in?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: If you can recognise the handwriting, then I'd like you to tell me both for the 4th and 5th of July and later on for the 14th and 15th -- between the 14th and 15th of June.

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I am quite certain that the handwriting of the third shift between the 4th and 5th of July, 1992 was that of my colleague Buba. That is to say Buba wrote the first bit, the first portion, and the addition, the additional portion, was written by Nada.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you say the first part, do you mean the part written in the Cyrillic script, up to the signature of those handing over the shift, Nada, Vesko and Buba?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is the portion I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And when you say the second part, the second part is written in the Latin script, is it not?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mrs. Pavlovic, is your handwriting on any of these shift reports? I'm not thinking about these two but generally in the book itself.

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't write into this book. I don't put entries into this book because I only do first shifts. So my handwriting won't be found in the book anywhere because I only do first shifts.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Does that mean that at that period of time you were never on duty in a second or third shift?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. That's what it means. From 1989 up until the present day, I have always worked on the first shift, only first shifts.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: In addition to this book, Mrs. Pavlovic, you have brought another book, and you said that it continues on from the 10th of July of that same year, and in that book I found no relevant information in view of the period, but why did you bring in that book?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I thought that it was a good idea to bring books in for the whole year. If we're talking about and discussing that particular year, I thought it would be a good idea for me to bring in the books for the whole year.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Mrs. Pavlovic, at your department was there special records or special -- a special book on operations, the operations performed by doctors at your department? Did you have a separate book for that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course, and that is the most important book of the department, and entries must be made for each patient if surgical intervention of any kind, no matter how small, was made. So all entries for all patients are made if any surgical intervention was made, whether it was surgery, the administration of a plaster cast, anything at all in the operations theatre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: The book that refers to that period you have also brought to The Hague; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have. And we are duty-bound by the laws of our country to store the book for ten years, keep the book for ten years. So the book is still a very important book which I must take back with me when I leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Would you take a look to see if this is the book. And I'm also going to ask you to look at the date of the 15th of June, 1992. But first take a look at the book itself and tell us is that the book that you have been describing and what dates the entries range from and the patients inscribed.

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is the book. In this book, entries are made of patients from the 16th of January, 1991, and the book goes on until the 10th of August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Would you read out the title of the book from page 1. What is the book called?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Protocol on operations or persons operated."

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Does that book relate exclusively to the orthopaedics department of the Uzice general hospital?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, just the orthopaedic department.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Would you now find the page on which entries were made for the 15th of June, 1992? And a photocopy of that page I am now going to hand over for the Court. I have already given copies in the original language to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, have you got a translation? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'll just point out that to read this translation you need to hold the pages side by side like this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mrs. Pavlovic, you have found the page, have you not?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Would you please slowly read out what it says from number 283? And it says "Information about the patient." That is written in Cyrillic. Would you read out everything it says and what the columns are, what the different columns are. Would you please do that for us now.

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ordinal number is 283, and the personal identification-registration number is 10004. The date is the 14th of June, 1992. It says: "Person operated: Filipovic Dragan from Visegrad," and his age -- date of birth, rather, is 1962. And then next after that it's under the ordinal number 284.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Would you please read on until the end. We don't need to have the clinical diagnosis but just the type of operation and the surgeon who operated. Read to the end of the column, please.

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have clinical diagnosis, that's the next column, the type of operation, which was performed by the surgeon, a description of what was actually done during the operation, the operating procedure, surgical procedure, what anaesthetic was administered. In this case it was a local anaesthetic. That's what it says. And the surgeon. And where it says, "Remarks," the instruments technician and the plaster technician, person who is in charge of instruments and plaster and their names. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mrs. Pavlovic, do you recognise which surgeon this was according to what is written here?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can read it out. I can't -- it says Dr. Jovicevic. That's what it says under "surgeon" or "operator."

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And the instruments nurse and plaster cast technician, are those people from your own department or from some other department who do that kind of work?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The plaster cast technician is from our department and the instruments nurse is from the operations theatre. She has nothing to do with our department. She is in the operating theatre department.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. When you read out the date in the third column, was that the date of the operation itself?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. It is the date when the surgery took place, when the operation took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Could you tell us what was the next operation and what day? What is the next operation according to the book and on what date did that occur?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The next -- the next operation was under the ordinal number of 284. The patient's identification-registration number was 10012, and the operation was performed on the 15th of June, 1992. Do you want me to read out the name?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, please, the name and the surgeon and the other technicians.

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The patient was Popovic Mirjana. She was from Ivancica. Her date of birth, the year she was born was 1945. The operation was performed by Dr. Gordic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And finally who attended the operation, what it says at the end?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milovan and Dragana. Dragana was the instruments technician and Milovan was the plaster cast technician.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you read out the next number, please, 284, but everything, from beginning to end, please.

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ordinal number 285 and the personal registration number was 10015. The date was the 15th of June, 1992. The patient operated on was Vasiljevic Mitar from Visegrad, born in 1954. The operation was performed by Dr. Gordic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I asked you, Mrs. Pavlovic, if you would, to read everything it says for this case, the clinical diagnosis and everything else, please.

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Clinical diagnosis, Fractura cruris laternus sinister. The operation that was performed, the type of operation, type of surgery, extensio, transcalcanearis laternus sinister.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Unfortunately, Mr. Domazet, most of the Latin terms are not being translated, which is understandable. The interpreters are not Latin speakers, but is there any way of getting a layman's interpretation of some of those medical terms?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps one of the next witnesses, a doctor, will be able to explain to us better, but, madam, with your knowledge and experience and being a nurse yourself, I hope you will be able to translate and explain the clinical diagnosis and the operation performed because the names are written down in Latin. So please, madam, if you are able to so would you go ahead and tell us. Let us look at the clinical diagnosis. Let's take that first.

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to leave that to the doctors from my department. They can do that better than me, if that is possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That's fair enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Would you tell me next, under ordinal number 6, in the column 6, what it says as to the operative findings.

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean 286?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: No. You were reading ordinal number 285, but just go along the columns and you come to column 6 which is the operative findings under number 6.

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A local anaesthetic was administered and a Kirschner pin is passed through -- was passed through the heel bone where, on the same bone, we place an extension apparatus with a weight of 7 kilogrammes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Is it 7? Would you look at the digits again, please.

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ah, yes. It says 7.5 kilogrammes. I think it says 7.5 kilogrammes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes. It's not legible enough. This brings us to column 7, Mrs. Pavlovic, and what does it say there?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says "Local," which means that the anaesthesia administered was a local one.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And, finally, column 13 with the remarks.

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't say who the surgeon was. It was Dr. Gordic. And in the remarks column it says, "Dragana," who was the instruments technician, a lady.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Was it the same instruments technician that assisted in the previous operation and in the next one, 286?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You see, there were three operations that were performed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: However, Mrs. Pavlovic, would this particular patient, Vasiljevic Mitar, it does not say Milovan as being the plaster cast technician. Does that mean that he did not take part or that no plaster cast was administered in this particular type of surgery?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A plaster cast is not administered when we place an extension, but as I say, our doctors will explain that better. But yes, a plaster cast was not administered on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you read out the next number on this page, 286, and the basic information that you have before you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ordinal number 286. Personal registration-identification number is 9133. The date was the 15th of June, 1992. The patient's name was Bugarin Rajko. He was from Priboj, born 1946.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: As far as that particular patient is concerned, could you just read out the name of the surgeon and who attended the surgeon during the operation?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The surgeon was Dr. Gordic, and attending the operation were Dragana and Milovan.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And would you read out the last column in this book. The number is 287, and the information which -- the same as you did for the previous patient.

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ordinal number is 287. The personal identification-registration number was 10179. The date was the 16th of June, 1992. The patient operated on was Moljevic, father's name Dusan, and patient's first name Andrija, from Visegrad, born 1959. The surgeon was Dr. Moljevic. In the remarks column, number 15, it says Tanja Maksimovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Pavlovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we continue, let me just note, Your Honour, that in the English translation it does not state that the surgeon's name was written in. Perhaps it wasn't legible enough. It's written in the Cyrillic. Or the name under 13, "remarks", which was also written in the Cyrillic, but they are to be found in the photocopy that I gave to Mr. Groome and the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mrs. Pavlovic, before I ask you something else about that page - so please stay with that page - would you tell me about the first number and patient, 283, Filipovic Dragan. The information relating to him, what script were they written in, Cyrillic or the Latin script?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean in this book here?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, 283, Filipovic Dragan, Visegrad. What script was the entry written in, the name, surname, and the address? Was that Cyrillic or Latin?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is written in the Cyrillic script.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And what about 284, is that Cyrillic or Latin?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 284 is written in the Latin script.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: 285, Vasiljevic Mitar?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 285, Latin script.

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 286, Latin script.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And finally, 287, please.

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 287, Cyrillic script.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: According to this book and what you read out, this first number written in the Cyrillic script, 283, was done on the 14th of June, 1992, was it not?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And numbers 284, 285, and 286, Popovic, Vasiljevic and Bugarin, all three operations are dated the 15th of June, 1992; is that right? And their names have been filled in, entered in in the Latin script; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: The operation under number 287 of the 16th of June, 1992, the entries there were in Cyrillic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I am now interested, Mrs. Pavlovic, in 284, 285, and 286, the operations performed on the 15th of June, 1992. Can you recognise the handwriting of the person who made the entries? Do you know who made the entries, the name and surname of the patient, and the first three columns?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can recognise 284, 285, and 286. That was written by my head nurse, the head nurse of the department, the ward, Mrs. Branka Djordjevic is her name. I recognised the handwriting because she has a characteristic and easily recognisable handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I should now like to tender, first of all, the shift book which Mrs. Pavlovic has brought with her and which relates to the relevant period, material time, that is to say, the 14th of June, 1992, be admitted into evidence. I think it would be D31.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Any objection, Mr. Groome?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: They will be Exhibit D31. That includes the English translations?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Then the surgical book?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should also like to tender that into evidence, but I'm afraid of -- bearing in mind what the witness said that this is an indispensable book for her department, although I think the time frame is expiring.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So I'd like to know, Mrs. Pavlovic, if that second book, the surgical book, could we keep the original?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you ask my doctors from my department, please, about that? I can leave this notebook and I'll be happy to do so, but us must ask the doctors from my department about the surgical book. I cannot give an answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, you remember that we discussed in relation to the other books that a photocopy would be made of them by somebody in the registry so that the hospital would have access to the photocopy whilst the original is put through whatever tests it has to be put through. Perhaps we can leave that to the doctors, but that's what I suggest should be done here because the Defence case clearly is one which -- I'm sorry, the Prosecution case is clearly one which creates a suspicion about the documents, these documents, and they are entitled to have them tested since they've only just been produced. But for the moment, it will be an exhibit. Whether it is exhibited or not, I see no problem with that. What about you, Mr. Groome?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: The book and the English translations will be Exhibit 32.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm sorry. That should be D32. I'm sorry about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, D32. Yes. Could the witness please be shown Exhibit P138, and in the B/C/S version, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Will you please look at the first page. Have you had time to look at the document? Could you tell us what this document is that you have in front of you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a case history, the document with which the patient comes to our department from the admissions department.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Is that the case history that you told us about when the patient is given his own personal registration number?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Where has it been entered in this document, and would you read it out, please?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under ordinal number 2, at the top right-hand corner, it says Maticni Broj or registration number, and I see it's been corrected. It's 10000. Now, whether it is 14 or 15, I can't tell. That is the last number.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So it says 10014 or 10015; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You mean that it is difficult to tell whether it is 4 or 5. The last digit has been corrected and one can't tell which it is, in fact?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Will you tell me what is written in the left-hand corner of the case history? Is it customary to enter that there, that is, not in the actual forms and columns?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to the VP number 985 and SUP informed?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: All. Everything that it says there.

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says, "VP 985, SUP informed. Injury on the front in Visegrad." And below that, "05 General hospital in Uzice, orthopedics department."

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Let us focus for a minute on the numbers you just read out. When it says -- there were some numbers, and it says "SUP informed." Could you tell us who would enter that information and for what reason?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, this is entered upon arrival at the hospital, upon admission. Now, why it is entered and who does it, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You mean about who has been informed that the patient has been admitted?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mrs. Pavlovic, will you look below that? It says, "On the battlefront in Visegrad." What does the term "battlefront" mean to you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, all the people who came from that area at that time, I noticed that on their case history this was written. Now, why that is so, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you said that all the people coming from the area, the area of Visegrad, they were the most frequent patients that came to your hospital, that it was noted that they were coming from the battlefront, is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you mean regardless of the injuries they had or how those injuries were inflicted?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, when a patient is, I don't ask him whether he waged war or not. For me, he's a patient. I don't have to think about those things at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Let me finish, please. Perhaps we didn't understand one another. This note from the battlefront in Visegrad was to be found on all case histories for patients coming from that area, regardless of their diagnosis, is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I assume so. Believe me, for my work that is irrelevant. It's something that doesn't interest me and I paid no attention to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Will you please look at the other entries and tell us which of those entries were made upon admission and which later on in your ward? Of course, if you can remember and on the basis of what you know from experience.

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll tell you the form the case history has when it reaches us and what is filled in upon admission.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes. Tell us what the regular procedure is and then you'll tell us whether this is an example of that.

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We receive the case history, as I have said, with the registration number entered, which is the number that is the most important for us, the date of admission, which is also important, especially for my surgical department because of the blood type, because that is attached to this number. These are the two pieces of information we attach the greatest significance to, in addition to the first and last name of the patient. Then the name of the patient, the name of the father of the patient, what kind of insurance he has, then also the entry regarding spouse, that is if he's married. If not, then the name of the parent. The address and the date of birth, you see it here. And that's it. That is what is important for us and those are the entries that are made upon admission. Sometimes it happens that they fill in the work he does and the occupation, but not on every case history. Sometimes they omit it. They leave it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Under entry 8, it says "Category of health insurance." Is that filled in?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We see underlined here "Military post." I don't know whether that is intentional or unintentional.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you know, Mrs. Pavlovic, whether the people who were brought from Visegrad and the treatment you gave them, was that paid for and who had to pay for it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I am really not familiar with that. That was something I never had any interest in.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you know the rest of the first page, the entries number 10 and 11, who fills those in and when? Do you know or what is the customary procedure, for -- if you're not certain about this particular case.

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is customary for the doctor to make the entries under 10 and 11. That is the customary procedure. But occasionally, we get a patient with number 10 filled in and sometimes, believe me, we get a patient with the wrong diagnosis from the admissions, but not always. So if you're asking me about the details. In that case, our doctor would correct it. So in any event, these entries are made by doctors.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mrs. Pavlovic, when you say the doctor corrects it, you mean if the doctor establishes that the original, initial diagnosis was not correct, and then under 11 he writes the proper diagnosis, the main cause being hospitalisation or final diagnosis? Do you know perhaps what entry 11, that is, the number at the end means, the number 8232 or 823.2 perhaps?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what it means.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mrs. Pavlovic, will you look at entry number 12 and the diagnosis there? Was that entry made in your department?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am unable to say because, as I said a moment ago, these are entries made by doctors.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And for entry 15, where it says "Date" and "Type of operation," who makes that entry and what does it say in this particular case history?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This entry is also made by the doctor, only by doctors. Shall I read out what it says?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's a date and the type of operation. Extensio transcalcanearis on the 15th of June, 1992. And then again in that same line, the 15th of June, 1992, I know that it is the duty of each doctor to make this entry on the case history.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Are these the data that you read out from the surgical book a moment ago about surgeries performed?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely those data regarding the type of operation and when it was performed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Let us go back for a moment once again to the top of this page. If you can see above entry number 1, there seem to be some initials, I think in Cyrillic, two letters. Could you tell us, on the basis your own knowledge, what these initials are?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We always write down the initials of the doctor who admitted the patient. As soon as he arrives at the department, we place the initials there. So in this case this is in Cyrillic, D and J, Dr. Dusko Jovicevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Would you please tell us to make sure whether this D is in Cyrillic or Latin script?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I find that it is Cyrillic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And in the top left-hand corner there's a number that seems to have been corrected. Could you remember what that number indicated?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The number stands for the number of the room, because the patient, as I told you earlier on reading out from the book, the patient was first admitted to room 413, and as soon as there was a vacancy in Dr. Dusko Jovicevic's room, 411, he was transferred to it, and that is why it has been made. This is not something very unusual. It happens very often.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So you recognise this number as the number of the room. It was first 413 and then the 3 was corrected to a 1 to make it 411. Will you please turn the page and look at the page where the interventions have been entered? Do you recognise the names or the signatures of the people working there? I think it is the third or fourth page. What has been entered on that page, Mrs. Pavlovic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can recognise the handwriting of my current head of department, Dr. Djordje Stojkovic. And on the 5th of July, 1992, at 9.00, 9.00 a.m., he requested a psychiatric examination. So upon finishing his regular round on the 5th of July, when I had to tell him what had happened during the night between the 4th and 5th, I had to brief him on events in the night, and that the patient, Mitar Vasiljevic, was worse than ever that night. That night, none of the patients could sleep. My colleague had noted that down in the notebook. He harassed the staff and the patients, and he demanded that a psychiatrist come to the ward.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You just said that "he" demanded. Who demanded a psychiatrist?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Stojkovic requested, because Dr. Stojkovic was the doctor making the rounds that morning. And in our institution, it is only a doctor that can ask for another doctor to come.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mrs. Pavlovic, you read this out and made your comments. That is the first note made on the 5th of July at 9.00 a.m. Could you identify the next note? Could you read it out and explain if you know what it Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. refers to?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can read it out. But at 2200 hours I wasn't there, but I'll read it out. On the 5th of July, 1992, at 2200 hours, and again it's Dr. Stojkovic, so I assume he was on duty that day. The requested examination by a neuropsychiatrist has not been performed. The patient continues to be restless, refusing to take his therapy, insulting the staff and patients. Dr. Stojkovic, typed out, and then his signature over there. It means that the psychiatrist did not come for the requested consultation. Why, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mrs. Pavlovic, you said you would read this out, because at the time you were not present. Does that mean that you were present on the 5th of July at 9.00 a.m. that you spoke about a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The nurse in charge of that area has to brief the doctor as to what had happened regarding each patient during the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, but my question was, when you read this out and made your comments, I had the impression that you were referring to what you personally remember about the incident. Am I right? Were you telling us about what you, yourself, recollect?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that patient, and I will remember him for a long time. That is why I'm here. If I didn't remember, I wouldn't have come.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So is it customary for you to make the rounds together with the doctors every morning?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, every morning when I'm working, if I'm not on annual leave or on sick leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Is that a convenient time, Mr. Domazet?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We'll adjourn now until 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Pavlovic, let's resume after the break. We were talking about the case history and what you read out from it, and we heard your comments. Now, you still have the exhibit in front of you, and please take a look at the third page now, page 3. You explained to us about the 5th of July and the event that took place that morning, and you read out what Dr. Stojkovic noted down that evening about that. Now, as there is no further indication that there was anything of note on the 6th of July, what can that mean? Can you comment?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there's nothing here. Nothing was written here. I assume that the patient got his discharge sheet and that he had completed his treatment, because I see that on the 7th of July, 1992, the patient -- it says: "The patient's discharge sheet was written out yesterday but the patient did not go home." Do you want me to read what it says to the end?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: No, thank you. There's no need. It's already in evidence. After that date, is there anything else that was filled in by your department?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The next piece of information which was written, I assume, by the doctor who came to -- for consultation, the psychiatrist. And finally, there is Dr. Moljevic's report of the 17th of July, 1992, where a consultation was held or, rather, an examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: It says, and please correct me if I'm wrong, it says, "Remark, control in one month's time, Tuesday mornings." Is that what it says?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Can you explain from your practice why it says "Tuesday morning," a set day of the week?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it would be best if you asked the doctors that. They would be able to explain that better, because each of them had a specific day when they were working in outpatients department, and each doctor was assigned a day of the week. I assume the doctor knows why he wrote that down. He will be able to tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: That's what I wanted to ask you about, work in the outpatients department. Does it mean that doctors from the department worked in the outpatients department as well, and if so, how much time did they spend?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Doctors from the department would work in the outpatients department, and each doctor had his own set day of the week when he would examine patients in the specialists' outpatients department.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Were the same nurses working in the outpatients department as worked in the department itself or were they different nurses?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Other nurses worked in the outpatients department. They work only in the outpatients. They were outpatient nurses. They don't come to the department and ward.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You, personally, at that time never worked in the outpatients department in the course of that year, did you? That would emerge from what you have explained to us so far.

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. I never, ever worked in the outpatients department.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Would you look at the second page of the discharge sheet. There are some entries written in the first half of the page and then the 15th of June and two other dates. Can you tell us something with respect to those first entries? Who makes those entries underneath the remarks, where it says "Urgent case"? Have you found that? "Emergency case."

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That information is entered by the doctor who received the patient upon admission, the same day that the patient is admitted. So he fills in the anamnesis. It is only the doctor that does that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And in this case, in this particular case, looking at the signature, that would have been Dr. Jovicevic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says "Dr. Jovicevic, ORP, orthopaedist."

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: On that same page, with respect to the operation, would you take a look and see if that is data about the surgery itself that you read out from the surgical book?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. And those entries are made by the doctor who performed the operation. So those are the facts I read out to you earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: The date is the 15th of June, 1992. That is the date of surgery; is that right? And what does the number represent?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The number is the surgical protocol number, and we write that number in, in our surgical book. Operations protocol.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you know, Mrs. Pavlovic, who made the other entries where it says the 8th of July and the 15th of July, those two entries, 8.7 and 15.7?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, but I can assume, judging from what I am able to see here, I think it was the psychiatrist. Which one, I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. That's all regarding that exhibit. But could we just go back to the operations book or surgical book that we were looking at, and number 285, when Mitar Vasiljevic was operated on. Have you got the page?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I think that you're still looking at the case history. Not the case history now, we've finished with that. I'm referring to the photocopy from the surgical book.

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't got it here. It's not on the table.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is Exhibit D32. Would the usher please hand the witness D32. The book itself would be best, the original book, please, so that you can take a look at the page that the operation was recorded on.

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've found it. Here it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You have it? You also have a case history that you were looking at a moment ago. Would you compare the two, please, now? In the surgical book, and the ordinal number is 285, look at that, please.

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: It says "Case history," and you read it out, and that's what it says in the book. The number is 10015. Now, on the case history, that is to say P138, Exhibit P138, in the upper corner you will see the number that you identified as being 10014 or 10015; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I can't quite determine the last digit. But as this was written in by my head nurse, I assume -- in the surgical book, what happens usually is she rings up to check. So it is the number that she entered into the surgical book.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. 10015 is the number that has been entered, but my question for you is the following: If the number was the number that you, yourself, couldn't read, whether it was 10014 or 10015, if that is the right -- if it was 10014, if the correct number should have been 10014, is the mistake then in the entry with respect to the number of the case history?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the case history number is in fact 10014 and it says here 10015, then that is a mistake when the entry was made, and I can't know that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Tell me this: The numbers, generally speaking, are they assigned in the order in which people come in or in some other way?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those numbers are only assigned according to the order in which they -- the patients were received, admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Have a look at that same page and look at patient 283, the number -- the ordinal number 283, and read his case history.

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His case history number is 10004. The patient's name is Filipovic Dragan.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Which means, does it, that he was admitted before Mitar Vasiljevic? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. He was admitted quite a bit earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Is the same thing true of 824, ordinal number 824?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Patient 284 was admitted before Mr. Vasiljevic, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, Mrs. Pavlovic. And a patient that was operated on the following day had a higher number. Perhaps it's a little unusual, but perhaps you can tell us. The patient under 286, who was operated the same day after Mitar Vasiljevic, has a number which is 9133, which is considerably lower, considerably lower number. Is that usual and what does it signify?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was admitted to hospital quite a lot before the rest. Now, why he was operated on only on that day, the doctor will best be able to explain that to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, madam, for your answer. I won't be asking you to look at the documents any more. I should now like to ask you to tell me something that you started talking about when you spoke about the rounds on the 5th of July. Will you tell me everything you remember, to the best of your recollections, about Mitar Vasiljevic for the period that you have been studying the documents? I think you've already told us, but let me ask you again, do you remember him as a patient?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I remember him very well. I remember the first morning when I met him best, because of -- that is to say, when I asked him how he was injured, I remember his specific answer, and it stuck in my mind once and for all. I thought he was joking at one point when he first said it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And what did he tell you? What did he say?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I asked the gentleman how he had injured himself, and he said, "My horse slipped and I broke a leg." And that was the first time that we had a patient, at least I had a patient, where a horse slipped and the man broke his leg.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So that was your first encounter. And if I understand you correctly, that was how you remembered him. Can you tell me anything else that you recall before the period of the 5th of July? Before the 5th of July, anything you remember before that, what his behaviour was like, whether he had any problems or whether you had any problems with him?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, his behaviour -- by his behaviour, he drew attention to himself while he was lying in bed at that time. I think all the patients in the ward knew him and all the staff working on the ward because his behaviour was rather unusual.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you say, Mrs. Pavlovic, that you think all the people on the ward knew him, patients and staff alike, can you tell us a little more about how they knew him?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I came to realise that when I would come on duty in the morning and I found a picture of a horse drawn on an ordinary piece of paper stuck up above his bed, and he would say, "A patient from the other wing drew that for me and stuck it up there," which means that even patients from different wings would come in and do things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, you're saying that patients would draw horses and stick it up on the wall by his bed; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. We never had a case like that before or after. People never did things like that. So the man did draw people's attention to himself and through incidents of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you happen to remember how he reacted to that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did you personally happen to see a drawing like that? Did you find a drawing like that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I took it down two or three times from the wall because I couldn't allow the doctor to come in on his rounds and see something like that. It was absolutely not allowed. So I took it off and threw it away. Yes, I did see it. And it is my job to prepare the dormitory, the room, and the patients at 7.30 for the doctors' rounds. So I had to do things like that, too, see that everything was neat and tidy.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: From what you say, this was repeated at least several times; is that right? Because you said that you took a drawing of that kind off the wall several times. Am I right in understanding that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's just how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mrs. Pavlovic, do you remember what the drawing was apart from the horse? You said that there was a drawing of a horse. Were the drawings different? Was anything else drawn in addition to the horse or were they always the -- was it always the same drawing?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I didn't study the drawings, nor was I interested in them. I just saw the horse. The horse was the dominant object, and I just took the papers down and threw them away. I can't say what else was on the pieces of paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you say, Mrs. Pavlovic, that it was your impression and knowledge that practically every patient knew of him, do you mean that everybody knew about that particular fact and incident, that he was injured by falling off a horse?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume so from the drawings of horses that they did. That is my assumption. That is what I assume. Why otherwise would they draw a horse except if he loved horses, liked horses especially? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Was Mr. Vasiljevic able to get out of bed? Was he mobile while he was on your ward?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic was not able to move from the moment the operation was conducted. He was 100 per cent immobile. What I want to say is he couldn't get out of bed at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Would you explain to us brief why, why that was?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he had been operated on and he was practically tied to his bed, because it's the kind of surgery which does not allow him to get up out of bed at all. He had weights hanging over -- from his leg, a Kirschner pin was stuck into his heel, so he wasn't able to get up.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Were they the weights, the weights that -- the weight of which you read out from the surgical book, the book of operations? You read out some weight. Were those the weights that weighted his leg?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. They were the weights.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Does that mean, Mrs. Pavlovic, that his leg -- that to his leg were affixed weights weighing approximately 7.5 kilogrammes and that that was one of the reasons that he was immobile, unable to move?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Therefore, he was a patient who could not and did not go out of his room throughout his stay in the orthopaedics ward; is that right? Have I understood that correctly?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you say that other patients knew about that, patients from other rooms, and that even some patients from another wing drew the drawings that were drawn, does that mean that the other patients who were mobile, who were able to move around, could go into his room, the room he was lying in?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume they could, yes. Patients who had an arm injury or hand injury, they were able to move around. And days are very long in hospital, you know, sir. Once the regular first shift work was over, that is the time that they would come to his room, during the second and third shifts.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mrs. Pavlovic, when you read portions from the case history and the note made by Dr. Stojkovic of the 5th of July, you said that that was noted down during his rounds and that he entered this into this case history. Now, as we're talking about the patients' behaviour, could you tell us, please, what you remember from that particular medical round, doctors' round, when all this happened, when the incident happened that Dr. Stojkovic made a note of in the case history.

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when my -- the colleague was taking over and when some incident occurred like the one connected to Mr. Vasiljevic, then the nurse must inform the doctor when he comes in on his rounds, and I informed him. And as you can see, the doctor immediately asked for a consultation with a psychiatrist.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did you prepare the visits, the doctors' rounds, or were there other nurses who were in charge of that, too?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The morning preparation for the rounds were done by all sisters on duty that morning. We would attend to the patients in our morning rounds. Now, who was on duty that morning with me, I just can't remember now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And who looks through the notebook to see what the previous shift, what the two previous shifts, that is to say, the second shift and third shift made a note of? Do the nurses look through those remarks or do the doctors do so?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the notebook that we were looking at a moment ago was

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: can also be reviewed by any of other colleagues who are interested in it, nurses, that is. Sometimes the head of the department would look through the notebook, but that's not the rule. It is our book. It is the notebook that we nurses keep. It is a nurse notebook.

utterances.speaker: THE HEAD NURSE OF
utterances.text: Tell me, please, this incident of the 5th of July is something you described for us, but do you remember that Mitar Vasiljevic acted in a similar manner even before this date? Do you happen to remember that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, I said a moment ago, that night he outstripped himself. All the time, he acted strangely. But he is one of many who acted in an unusual manner in those days.

utterances.speaker: THE HEAD NURSE OF
utterances.text: When you said he outdid himself, you mean he overdid it, that he had acted similarly before but not to such an extent?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He really went too far and it was recorded.

utterances.speaker: THE HEAD NURSE OF
utterances.text: To the extent to which you were able to see him, I mean, did you see him every day, of course on the days that you were working?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which was working, I would see him, of course. He was always in the same bed, in the same place, while he was hospitalised in the orthopedics ward.

utterances.speaker: THE HEAD NURSE OF
utterances.text: Because you said that he was there all the time, the people who were with him in the same room, did they change? Do you remember how big the room was, how many beds there were in it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember because all our rooms were the same then and they are today. We openly have rooms with four beds. So there were four beds. We don't have larger rooms than that. There is a room with three beds, two or three rooms with three beds, and that's it.

utterances.speaker: THE HEAD NURSE OF
utterances.text: So the largest room is a room with four beds, and he was in one of those rooms?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE HEAD NURSE OF
utterances.text: Do you remember a patient who was with him in the same room and that he had some problems with Mitar Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that night, the night we have mentioned, that is the 5th. That night he was with a patient of Muslim ethnicity and faith, but only that night, as far as I know. And then it was noted that he harassed the patient. He harassed the nurses. I can even remember the name of that patient because it's a patient who was lying in our ward for four months or roughly so. Approximately that long.

utterances.speaker: THE HEAD NURSE OF
utterances.text: Could you tell us who that was and why he was lying in your ward?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The patient's name was Selim Lepenica, whose leg had been amputated, and he was Dr. Dusko Jovicevic's patient. I know that he stayed in our hospital until he found some appropriate accommodation elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: THE HEAD NURSE OF
utterances.text: According to your best recollection, was he there before Mitar Vasiljevic came to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, much earlier. And he stayed on after Mitar left our ward. He was a patient who was hospitalised for a long time and that is why I remember him. And he very often calls us. I'm sorry, I didn't bring his letters. He writes to us from Munich. Quite recently, he wrote from Sarajevo. He thanks us for our care.

utterances.speaker: THE HEAD NURSE OF
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. I gather from what you've said that the patient was being treated before Mitar Vasiljevic arrived and that he left the hospital after Mitar Vasiljevic was moved. How serious were his injuries and what kind of care was he given, considering such a long period of hospitalisation?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can say is that he was immobile regarding the work that we nurses did. I can tell you about that. As for his injuries, you must ask the doctors. I just know that he was immobile, with amputated leg. How serious the injury was, you must ask the doctors.

utterances.speaker: THE HEAD NURSE OF
utterances.text: In the course of his stay, and I am referring to the patient Lepenica, did he complain about your personal treatment of him or the treatment he was given by the other nurses?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you what he would say to me every day when I administered therapy or dressed his wounds. He always expressed his gratitude and blessed me. As for others, I can only assume, but he writes to us quite frequently. He sends his greetings. He wishes us all the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. best, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: THE HEAD NURSE OF
utterances.text: When you said, "He blessed me personally every day," could you say exactly which words he used, what exactly you meant?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was extremely grateful, to put it in a nutshell. He was grateful for my attitude towards him, and I think very fact that he spent such a long time with us is indicative. And all of us nurses did our best to make his stay as comfortable as possible, because after all, he was there for a long time.

utterances.speaker: THE HEAD NURSE OF
utterances.text: When you say, Mrs. Pavlovic, that you later received letters from Munich and Sarajevo from him, did you personally, or the other nurses, I mean, was it addressed to somebody in person or all of you?
