utterances.text: So we should expect, if we had the first shift book, we should expect to see the note about his surgery in that book; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the doctor didn't tell the nurse in the third shift that that would be done in the course of the first shift, she has no right to record it. That means that he didn't say anything. He didn't say when he intended to do it. Had he said -- had he told the nurse, the nurse would have had to have recorded it in the takeover of duty book.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The book that we have that records the shift information records information from the second and third shift; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: We don't have the book here in court for the first shift; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That book doesn't exist. It's not kept. It's not recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So that there is no book where what happens on the first shift is recorded?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. What is done in the first shift, we have the protocol, this protocol here. And the results, I mentioned that, we have a results notebook in which all the patients are recorded and what the laboratory is asked to do, the laboratory tests and findings. That book exists. Then there is a book of the consultations asked for, for certain patients, and that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: When I first began to ask you questions, there were about five or six different things that were recorded in these shift books. Certainly, not all of those six are recorded in the operation protocol; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In the surgical protocol, the operation is recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And was there ever a time that a shift book for the first shift was maintained in the orthopaedic ward?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I have been working, no, but there is a consultations notebook in which we record, enter for each patient. If a psychiatrist was called, it is recorded. If an internal medicine specialist was called in, it is recorded. And there is another notebook in which we enter all the patients' names that are patients admitted. That is written in the first, second, and third shift those entries are made. So every single patient who was admitted, it says name, surname, and then take such-and-such from the laboratory, and at the end, the patient identification number. That is all that is done in the first shift.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: This admissions book that you're talking about now, is that the same book you were referring to a few minutes ago?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: A few minutes ago you referred to an orthopaedic admittance book. Is this the same book that you're telling us about now or is this a different book?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the results notebook, the findings, the results. That's what we call it. And on the front page, it says "Notebook of results," and in that notebook we make entries of every patient coming to the department. What the doctor -- what analysis the doctor has asked for and the patient identification number, in addition to the name and surname.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In the orthopaedic ward, is there a typewriter there that is used by doctors to type up the notes on the case history?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And how many typewriters were there in 1992, more than one?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I really can't remember. I know that we always have too few of them, always, always a shortage. Sometimes a doctor has to wait for his colleague to type something out. We haven't got too many of them, that's for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you tell us with certainty that there was more than one at the time of 1992, summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't say so, but perhaps only one was in working order. It was a very long time ago. It's very difficult for me to remember things like that now, and I wouldn't like to say something that I'm not absolutely sure of.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And am I correct in thinking that the -- each department in the hospital had its own typewriter to do its own notes on case histories?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. You're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to show you one of the medical records. It's P137. You did not bring this, but it is one of the records from Uzice hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: This document has never been translated but I do have copies for the Court if the -- if it's convenient for the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to ask you to look at the entry in this protocol book with ordinal number 188. Do you see that entry?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And who is that -- what is the name of person --

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: -- in that entry?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume it is Mitar Vasiljevic. This "Vasiljevic" isn't too legible, but yes, Vasiljevic Mitar, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, am I correct in saying that according to this protocol book, Mr. Vasiljevic was the last patient recorded on the 14th of June?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And can I ask you to just read across the entry for Mr. Vasiljevic? I believe it's the last column, but I'm not absolutely sure. But does that entry indicate somebody who was notified of Mr. Vasiljevic's hospitalisation?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the last column it says, "SUP informed," and then it says, "V police," and the number is 985. "V police," and 985.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Does that number mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is it possible that "V police" stands for military police? Did you ever see that abbreviation?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Pavlovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Re-examination, Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do have, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When we are looking at this document -- keep it, please, in front of you, Exhibit 137, and will you please look at the first column which goes from 184 to 193; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And 184. Will you tell us what the time of admission was, the date and hour?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For number 184, he was recorded on the 13th of June, 1992, at 1630 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And the last entry on this page under number 193?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only see, under 193, that the date is the 15th of June, 1992, but I can't see the time. There's no time. There is -- not on my copy. I can't see anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I think it's 1540. It can barely be seen. But tell me regarding the last column, from the top to the bottom, in all these cases, will you see what it says? Is it right to say that in all these cases the SUP, the military police, and what is known as 985 were informed?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that. All the admitted patients, we see that it says in the last column that the SUP and the military police have been informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Would you agree that in some cases it just says, "All informed"?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. For 189, it says "Informed all."

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And then when you see Mitar Vasiljevic's entry under number 188 and his admission to the hospital at 2135 hours, will you see when the previous person was admitted?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. 187, on the 14th of June, 1992, at 1540 hours. The name is Dragan Filipovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Does it say to which department he was admitted or sent to?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Admitted to the orthopaedic department. It says that in the seventh column, column number 7, "Admitted to orthopedics."

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mrs. Pavlovic, is that the Dragan Filipovic whose name you read out as having been admitted in the second shift on the 14th of June and who was operated? You found him in the operations book of Dr. Jovicevic on the 14th, and on the 15th, in the morning, you took his results. Is that the same person?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Dragan Filipovic, who was admitted before the mentioned Mitar Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Just one further point in this connection. You were looking at a photocopy with the dates and times. Do you know which book this sheet was taken from or photocopied from?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can just assume, because I've never seen this book in real life. These data are entered only in the admissions department of a hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions regarding that exhibit. I have a few more questions relevant to questions put to you by Mr. Groome. In answer to Mr. Groome's question as to when you began to notice something in Mr. Vasiljevic's behaviour, you said, and I took that down, on page 50 you said, and I'm quoting: "From the very beginning, I noticed that something was wrong with him." Do you remember having said that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And you also said that you heard a lot from your colleagues about it. So I assume they were colleagues from your shift or from other shifts? Could you tell us what it is that you heard from your colleagues?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, we do have the shift book, but we also hand over our shift orally because that nurse cannot leave until the first shift arrives, and she has to be told what happened. Then every nurse briefs the incoming nurse, not just about Mitar Vasiljevic but regularly. So that I would hear -- not just me but all of us -- comments about his behaviour, whether he was restless, whether he harassed anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: What you heard from your colleagues in addition to what you personally noticed and heard, did that lead you to make the conclusion that you did which I read out a moment ago, and that is that you said that you noted from the beginning that something was wrong with him?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you quite frankly and informally, he seemed to me not quite normal, quite lost and not quite normal. But I'm saying that as a layman. Because one cannot break a leg and then sing. To me, that is abnormal.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Very well, Mrs. Pavlovic. Mr. Groome drew your attention to an exhibit, D31, this is a notebook of shifts, and asked you to look at the second shift for the 14th of June. Do you have that notebook with you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You found the 14th of June?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: In answer to Mr. Groome, you said that there was something missing in the note of that shift. If I understood correctly is that the names were not entered of the people who were in that shift, as we mostly find in other cases. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Apart from that, apart from the fact that on that page we don't see the names of the nurses or technicians who were there, does the report regarding that day have any other shortcomings?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. All I can conclude from this note is that they were very busy that day. This probably doesn't mean anything to you, but the report tells me that they were working in the operating theatre, that they had admissions, one, two. So I think there are no shortcomings. They were tired.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: One further question regarding that date. Was that the shift and date when this patient that we mentioned a moment ago was admitted, Dragan Filipovic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is the shift that admitted Dragan Filipovic to the ward, the second shift on the 14th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mrs. Pavlovic, asked by Mr. Groome about Dr. Jovicevic and a possible other doctor on duty in the night of the 14th of June, you said that it was Dr. Jovicevic and that it can be seen from the fact that he admitted this patient. But he also said that Dr. Jovicevic was the director of the hospital at the same time. My question is, when Dr. Jovicevic was performing the duties as director of the whole hospital of the general hospital in Uzice; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Was he at the same time working as a doctor in the ward and performing operations?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And like other doctors, did he have the duty to be on duty for 24 hours like other doctors?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mrs. Pavlovic, did that mean that apart from the time when he was working in the ward or being on duty, that sometimes he had to be absent from the ward to perform the duties he had as the director of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. That was not something that interested me. So his colleagues will probably be able to tell you something about that. They certainly had to do a lot of those things instead of him. Now, what their internal arrangements were, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Would it happen, Mrs. Pavlovic, that in the case of an emergency, an urgent case, that in addition to the doctor on duty, another doctor may be called in to assist?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean an orthopaedic surgeon? You are referring to the wartime year?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes. I'm referring to 1992.

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was always another orthopaedist in the admissions department as member of this triage group.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You're talking about the triage department. That is the admissions department which has no physical link to the orthopaedics department where Dr. Jovicevic was on duty?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So at the admissions triage department, there was also an orthopaedist who was on duty who took part in the admissions?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was a member of the team, together with the other surgeons, general surgeons or of whatever other speciality. As far as I know, there was an orthopaedist as well, but the doctor will explain that better than I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Those doctors who were working in the triage group, be they surgeons or orthopaedists, were they doctors who were from that hospital working in their respective departments or were they doctors who were employed somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They were doctors of the general hospital, if I understood your question properly. Do you mean whether doctors were called in from other clinics or hospitals? I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Let me try and make it quite clear. The doctors working in the triage team at the admissions part of the hospital which you said consisted of surgeons and orthopaedists, were they the same doctors who were working in the various departments of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were the same doctors.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mrs. Pavlovic, Mr. Groome asked you to look at this notebook and Exhibit D31, and he drew your attention to certain dates and certain parts of that notebook which are either untidy, with pages falling out or something like that. I didn't notice that his remarks related to this particular period, but will you please open the page relating to the 14th and the 15th of June, please?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Will you look at those pages, please, a few pages before and a few pages after. Are there any irregularities on those pages which you did notice on some other pages that Mr. Groome drew your attention to?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be quite sincere, I see no irregularities except for the fact that the names were not noted down in the second shift for the 14th of June, as we said a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: In those days, was there any other nurse with the name Slavica in the orthopaedics department?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to think about it, because now there are 6 of us left out of the 25, 6 who were working at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Can you remember whether there's another Slavica working, there was another Slavica working?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know, it's a very common name in our country. There were 20 nurses, and many have left.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Never mind. If you remember, you'll tell me. Let me ask you something else. Who would decide on the transfer of patients from one room to another?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only the doctor could decide, the doctor who admits a patient and possibly the head nurse in the department. But only the doctor could tell us to move a patient to such-and-such a room. But every doctor had his own patients' room, that is, the room where his patients were lying.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: The head nurse, as far as I can remember, her name was certainly not Slavica.

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Her name was Branka Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I'm asking you this so as to avoid any misunderstanding in my questions and your answers, because Mr. Groome is right when he told you that in the statement of Selim Lepenica that you, too, mentioned, that in the statement to the investigator you were not mentioned, but you were mentioned twice in his statement to the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That is why I asked you about that, and I wouldn't like you to have the impression that I had said something that is not correct, because you are mentioned and two other nurses, Sladjana and Zorica, but there's no need to go into that in detail as I have been advised that that is irrelevant. One more question. In answer to a question from Mr. Groome, you said that there was a notebook of results, and I understand that it contained quite a lot of information from the first shift during regular working hours. Do you know whether that notebook still exists that relates to 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does, but that notebook is so disorderly. When this one appeared to Mr. Groome as something in very bad shape, I wonder what the impression he will get to see the other one. So it does exist, but it's in very bad shape and untidy.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you say it's untidy, what do you mean? Is it the original book?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Has it been corrected or is it just the condition of the pages?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant the condition of the pages, the various handwritings. The impression is a very bad one, but it is an authentic notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Pavlovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you, madam, very much for coming along to give evidence and for the evidence which you've given. You are now free to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Rather than try to start another witness this afternoon, I thought it might be just as well if we cleared up a few of these outstanding issues. Mr. Groome, have you seen the expert witness for criminal law which has been filed?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: We received a copy yesterday, Your Honour. I haven't had a chance to read it yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: When you do, a great deal of it is strictly irrelevant as to what the criminal law is, but it may be of assistance if we ever got to the stage of looking at particular sentences to know what Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the nature of the crimes were that they were sentenced for. The relevant part is the sentencing practices, which we're obliged to have some regard to, but it's all very usual sorts of things, something I have read before, a great deal of it. I'm hoping that we will not need to bring this witness along. You better have a look at it from that point of view as to whether you need to cross-examine him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now, the writing samples. What's happening about all of this?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I must apologise to the Court again. I was not able to look at the documents either this morning or at lunch. I will look at them after court today, and we still have not been able to reach the forensic examiner. We've tried every day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I wonder if there is another one available because we can't wait forever.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It's just that this one is just a few miles away so it avoids a lot of the problems that we would have. So if I don't hear from him by the end of tomorrow, we'll seek to identify another forensic examiner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: The Netherlands has a population of 16 million people. I'm sure it has more than one competent document examiner. But there are two matters which follow from this: First of all, I think that at some stage arrangements will have to be made within the registry to photostat these documents so that the hospital will have access to those records until we can return the books, and we can't do that unless they've got the books. So if you're still looking at them, they can't get on to that particular thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm return them in the morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And the other thing is this last book, the surgical one, it seems to have some particular importance to it. Perhaps some priority can be given to that so that that can be returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You are, of course, still to nominate the periods in each of these particular books that you want to have examined by the document examiner, and I think we should have a record of that somewhere which ones you are having so that Mr. Domazet, if he wishes, can suggest other portions as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Just so it doesn't have to be done twice, that's all. Now, is there anything you want to raise before we perhaps have an early afternoon?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Not for the Prosecution, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: How about you, Mr. Domazet?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour, perhaps this is a good opportunity for us to discuss the timetable, since we have another four witnesses who are present, and tomorrow evening, the last two should arrive. According to the progress we are making, it seems to me that by Monday or Tuesday, we will have finished with the examination of witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You don't think that's being just a little optimistic, do you? At the rate we're going, I would have thought it might take a little longer than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm not criticising anyone because these documents are very important from both parties' points of view, and they necessarily require a great deal of attention. But who are the other doctors or who are the other witnesses who are coming? You've been dropping some off, I gather, along the way.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. Unfortunately, another witness has cancelled. At least, he is not able to come during the dates we would have liked to hear him, and it is Dr. Djordje Stojkovic, precisely the doctor that was frequently mentioned by the witnesses. He's unable to come on Friday or next week, and that is a problem. So if there's no way we can deal with that, we'll have to drop him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Except that there is the Monday and the Tuesday of the following week, is there not? You see, the sitting has to finish on the Tuesday of the last week because there is a Plenary meeting of the Judges for three days.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I don't want there to be a very long period if we can avoid it between your witnesses, because the Prosecution obviously will have somebody in reply, if only in relation to the X-ray issue. Anyway, we can look at that one again at the beginning of next week, remembering that we won't be sitting on Thursday of next week. Now, about your case in reply, if you're able to give us any indication, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm still trying to make a determination and evaluation of what the Prosecution will call in reply, but in relation to what Mr. Domazet has said, I am making efforts to bring witnesses at the end of next week. It seems it will probably be prudent for me to put those on hold until we make a final decision about Dr. Stojkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I agree. I would not like the Defence case to suffer if only it means that we will be sitting for a few days taking evidence perhaps at the beginning of next term, subject to the Serbian Christmas Day, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I can say to the Court at this stage that I cannot imagine that the reply case will be more than a week and it probably will be less than a week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I hope so. The most important thing I want to emphasise yet again is that the written submissions should be well under way. We just cannot give you a week or so off to do those. They should be well under preparation now. Whatever days we're not sitting next week, those should be taken advantage of to keep going on those written submissions, and of course during the vacation. When we do have a case in reply, my suggestion is that the submissions be made in relation to those -- that evidence, they can be made orally. We need to get on to the case and get it concluded, otherwise, there are going to be two very real problems. One of our members has to start another case, I think on the 21st of January, and there is no way that we can really expect anybody to sit in two cases at the same time. I know the Prosecutor had certain views about that, but they have proved to be utterly discredited by attempts made in both tribunals to follow that practice. The other thing is we only have three courtrooms and there will be six trials running next year throughout the whole year, and unless you want to go to Utrecht, we won't be able to hear the case. Indeed, I think even the Utrecht or the Camp Zeist courtroom is being used for the appeal in the Lockerbie case during January, so we are in a lot of trouble. All right. So on that grim warning, we will adjourn now and resume at 9.30 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
